- **The real layout of the world (continents, oceans, sea routes)** [`world_geography`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/world_geography.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Dutch atlases and Jesuit reports from China and America are in court and monastery libraries. Australia's east, the north Pacific and the interiors are blank. Vienna has no overseas trade. Local: Hofbibliothek (Blaeu atlases); Jesuit college (mission letters). Elsewhere: Amsterdam: map publishers; Paris: Cassini's world map at the Observatoire.
- **Global wind belts and ocean currents (trade winds, westerlies, volta do mar, monsoon)** [`wind_systems_ocean_currents`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/wind_systems_ocean_currents.md) — K2, use none, make impossible, accept medium. Known from voyage accounts only; irrelevant to a Danube city. Halley's chart of the trade winds appears in 1686. Elsewhere: Dutch, English, Portuguese and Spanish pilots.
- **Magnetic compass** [`magnetic_compass`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/magnetic_compass.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Used by surveyors and mine surveyors, and for setting sundials. Local: instrument makers and compass-sundial makers; mine surveyors of the Lower Hungarian mining towns.
- **Magnetic variation (declination) and deviation** [`magnetic_declination`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/magnetic_declination.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Surveyors correct for declination. That it drifts over the years is in print (Gellibrand, 1635) but local values are rarely re-measured. Elsewhere: London and Paris: regular measurements.
- **Dead reckoning (course, speed, time; log line and traverse table)** [`dead_reckoning_log_line`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/dead_reckoning_log_line.md) — K2, use none, make easy, accept medium. A seaman's method known from books. Danube boatmen steer by landmarks and by knowledge of the channel.
- **Latitude from Pole Star and noon Sun (quadrant, astrolabe, cross-staff, kamal)** [`latitude_astrolabe_quadrant`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/latitude_astrolabe_quadrant.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Jesuit mathematicians and surveyors take the latitude with quadrants; gunners use a quadrant for elevation. Local: Jesuit college, mathematics professors.
- **Reflecting instruments (octant, sextant)** [`reflecting_octant_sextant`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/reflecting_octant_sextant.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept medium. Hooke showed a reflecting instrument in London in 1666; nothing came of it. Good flat mirrors and a finely divided arc are the bottleneck. Elsewhere: London: Hooke's proposal (1666).
- **Longitude by lunar distances** [`longitude_lunar_distances`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/longitude_lunar_distances.md) — K1, use none, make very-hard, accept medium. Proposed in books since 1514. The Moon's motion is not known well enough. On land, longitude is being found from Jupiter's moons. Elsewhere: Greenwich: Flamsteed's observatory (1675); Paris: Cassini's tables of Jupiter's moons (1668).
- **Longitude by marine chronometer** [`longitude_chronometer`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/longitude_chronometer.md) — K1, use none, make very-hard, accept medium. The idea is in print. Huygens' sea trials of pendulum and spring clocks failed in rough water. Elsewhere: The Hague and Paris: Huygens; London: Hooke, Tompion.
- **Nautical charts and map projections (portolans, Ptolemy, Mercator)** [`map_projection_charts`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/map_projection_charts.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Mercator's projection is known from atlases. Local work is land survey: Vischer's map of Lower Austria and the engineers' plans of the fortress. Local: Georg Matthäus Vischer (Lower Austria 1670, Topographia 1672); Daniel Suttinger (plans of Vienna). Elsewhere: Amsterdam: sea charts.
- **Sounding lead, rutters and coastal pilotage** [`sounding_lead_pilotage`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/sounding_lead_pilotage.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Danube pilots sound with poles and know the shifting gravel bars and the Strudengau rapids by heart; nothing is charted. Local: Danube boatmasters (Schiffmeister) and pilots (Nauführer).

Galileo's and Descartes' explanations compete; none is right. No tide within many days' travel. Elsewhere: English and Dutch ports: tide tables.

- **Ocean-going ships (carvel hull, sternpost rudder, mixed square and lateen rig)** [`ship_design_caravel_carrack`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/ship_design_caravel_carrack.md) — K2, use none, make very-hard, accept medium. Local: boatbuilders and Schiffmeister on the Danube arm (Rossau, Leopoldstadt). Elsewhere: Dutch, English, French and Venetian yards.

- **Watertight bulkheads** [`watertight_bulkheads`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/watertight_bulkheads.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept medium. River boats are open and cheap, often used for one trip. Boatbuilders see no reason to divide a hull.
- **Shipworm and copper sheathing** [`copper_sheathing_shipworm`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/copper_sheathing_shipworm.md) — K1, use none, make medium, accept low. No shipworm in fresh water. Copper comes from Neusohl in Upper Hungary and is a war material. Elsewhere: Sea powers: lead or sacrificial wood sheathing.
- **Provisioning and keeping crews alive on long voyages** [`ship_provisioning_long_voyages`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/ship_provisioning_long_voyages.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. The local form of the problem is the siege: flour, salt meat and wine are stored. Scurvy and dysentery are blamed on bad air and salt food. Local: city provision office and imperial Proviantamt.

- **Diving bell and underwater work** [`diving_bell`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/diving_bell.md) — K2, use none, make medium, accept medium. Described in the Jesuit Schott's Technica curiosa (1664). No one in Vienna has built one; river salvage uses hooks and divers. Elsewhere: Stockholm: guns raised from the Vasa by diving bell (1660s).
- **Canals and pound locks** [`canal_locks`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/canal_locks.md) — K2, use none, make hard, accept medium. Pound locks are known from Italy, the Netherlands and France. The unregulated, braided Danube and the lack of money prevent any project. Elsewhere: France: Canal du Midi (opened 1681); Brandenburg: Friedrich-Wilhelm Canal (1668); Lombardy and the Netherlands.
